title: What is a pangram? The quick brown fox has a job
description: A sleepy dog, a jumping fox and all 26 English letters. Discover the trick inside this familiar sentence—and the tiny edit that breaks it.

cover.alt: Handmade brown fox jumping over a sleeping cream dog, with Q, X and Z letter tiles
cover.credit: AI-generated cover image created for BrainiLab.

practice: Keep looking for hidden patterns in words with Connections.

sections.title: A fox with a surprisingly useful job
sections.html:
A pangram is a sentence or phrase that uses every letter of an alphabet at least once. For the English alphabet, that means all 26 letters. Merriam-Webster gives this definition.

Meet the famous example: “The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.” It sounds like a wildlife report from someone with very little happening that afternoon. Yet the fox is doing more than annoying a dog.

sections.title: Where are the awkward letters?
sections.html:
Look for the letters you might otherwise leave out. There is a q in quick, an x in fox and a z in lazy. The less conspicuous letters are there too.

Ignore spaces and the full stop: the sentence has 35 letters, but 26 different letters. That is allowed. A pangram needs to include the alphabet; it does not have to use each letter only once.

sections.title: Why does it keep turning up on screens?
sections.html:
A pangram gives you a compact sample of the whole alphabet. That makes it handy for trying a typeface: you can see how its letters look inside words rather than in an A-to-Z parade.

Wordsmith also describes using pangrams for typing practice. One short sentence makes you reach for every alphabetic key. The fox has found steady work.

sections.title: One tiny edit breaks the trick
sections.html:
Change jumps to jump. Which letter disappears from the sentence?

S. There is no other s to cover for it, so the edited sentence is no longer a pangram. Keeping the story almost unchanged is not enough; the letter rule decides.

This is a different challenge from an anagram, which rearranges an existing set of letters. Try writing your own pangram: start with a sensible sentence, then hunt for the letters still missing. The rare ones tend to demand the strangest guests.

questions.prompt: What must an English pangram include?
options: The same letters forwards and backwards
questions.explanation: It must contain every letter of the English alphabet. Repeated letters are allowed.

questions.prompt: Can a pangram repeat a letter?
options: Yes, if every alphabet letter is still included
questions.explanation: At least once means repeats are fine. The famous fox sentence has 35 letters but 26 different letters.

questions.prompt: Change jumps to jump in the famous fox sentence. Which alphabet letter is now missing?
questions.explanation: The only s was in jumps. Removing it leaves the sentence without an s.
